content: Cytokine responses can have significant metabolic effects, including reduced appetite and food intake, depletion of carbohydrate stores, loss of minerals and micronutrients, protein-losing enteropathy due to serum protein leakage across damaged mucosa into the gut lumen, muscle protein breakdown, and a shift in hepatic protein synthesis from albumin to acute-phase proteins that support host defense mechanisms. These effects often persist well beyond the acute phase of illness, contributing to ongoing loss of lean body mass during recovery. When successive infections—whether enteric, respiratory, or systemic, and caused by viral or bacterial pathogens—occur in rapid succession, especially when accompanied by fever that exacerbates catabolic losses, nutritional deficits cannot be adequately restored. This leads to a progressive decline in nutritional status, ultimately resulting in severe protein-energy malnutrition. Without timely nutritional interventions, death is a common outcome. This scenario is particularly prevalent among children under five years of age in developing countries, where repeated infections deplete nutrient stores without sufficient time for recovery before the next infection occurs. Consequently, malnutrition is associated with over half of childhood deaths and remains a major risk factor even when a specific terminal illness is identified. Enteric infections are significant contributors to this progressive nutritional decline and are often the underlying cause of death, regardless of the terminal event. The delayed effects of enteric diseases, particularly inflammatory diarrhea, are frequently underestimated when assigning causes of death, leading to an underappreciation of their overall disease burden. Recent studies of inpatient deaths suggest that standard anthropometric methods underestimate the impact of malnutrition, with malnutrition accounting for more than 50% of attributable risk of death. The synergistic interaction between malnutrition and infectious diseases remains a valid framework for understanding this relationship. The outlook is concerning, as population growth in many developing countries continues unabated, and the effects of climate change and extreme weather events increasingly threaten soil quality, food supply, and nutritional status. These factors undermine efforts to reduce poverty, improve nutrition, and enhance general health. Food insecurity remains a major global crisis, contributing to approximately 9 million deaths annually, second only to acute pneumonia as a cause of death in children under five years of age. The highest proportion of under-five deaths due to diarrheal disease occurs in the South-East Asia and Africa regions of the World Health Organization (WHO). Diarrheal diseases, particularly those caused by rotavirus and Shigella species, are leading causes of mortality in young children. Rotavirus infections, primarily affecting infants under two years of age, are responsible for up to 25% of diarrheal deaths due to rapid dehydration. Shigella infections, which are less responsive to rehydration therapy, also contribute significantly to mortality, with persistent diarrhea accounting for 30–50% of diarrheal deaths. Despite these challenges, mortality from enteric infections in young children has decreased over the past 30 years, largely due to the success of oral rehydration therapy, recognition of persistent diarrhea as a problem, nutritional rehabilitation programs, and micronutrient supplementation. However, there are several caveats to interpreting these data. Limited information exists on the prevalence of inflammatory diarrhea and dysentery, and sustaining the effectiveness of antibiotics for bloody diarrhea is a growing concern due to bacterial resistance. Additionally, while nutritional status and access to care have improved in some regions, the incidence of diarrhea in children under five has not decreased over the past three decades. Any deterioration in health systems, environmental sanitation, or access to safe water, as well as treatment failures due to antimicrobial resistance, could reverse current favorable trends. Cholera remains a significant public health challenge, with global trends showing a steady increase in reported cases. Underreporting of cholera is common, particularly in regions with inconsistent case definitions and limited laboratory support. Similarly, Shigella dysenteriae Type 1, which has caused devastating epidemics in the past, remains a concern in humanitarian crises and emergencies, where enteric infections can account for over 40% of reported deaths, predominantly in children under two years of age. Zoonotic diarrheal diseases, such as those caused by non-typhoidal Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7, Campylobacter jejuni, and Cryptosporidium parvum, are also significant contributors to the global burden of disease. These pathogens often colonize animal hosts without causing disease but can lead to severe foodborne illness in humans. In the United States, foodborne illnesses are estimated to cause 76 million new cases annually, resulting in 325,000 hospitalizations and 5,000 deaths, with an economic burden of $152 billion per year. Emerging zoonotic infections, such as bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis, remain underrecognized despite their potential contribution to the human tuberculosis epidemic, particularly in the context of HIV/AIDS. Limited laboratory diagnostic capacity and lack of awareness among clinicians hinder accurate identification of these infections. Similarly, anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis, poses a significant threat in endemic regions, with high case-fatality rates for pulmonary and gastrointestinal forms of the disease. Rabies, a viral disease that is almost universally fatal once clinical signs appear, remains a major public health problem in many developing countries, particularly in Africa and Asia. More than 90% of human rabies cases result from contact with rabid dogs. Despite progress in some regions, rabies continues to disproportionately affect children, who are more likely to be bitten and sustain injuries in high-risk areas such as the head and neck. Community-led interventions, such as the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC), have demonstrated the value of empowering communities to take responsibility for health interventions. These programs have not only controlled diseases like onchocerciasis but also improved overall health, school attendance, and food production. Community participation is essential for achieving sustainable improvements in sanitation and reducing the burden of zoonotic diseases.
